label: When You Have Lost Hope
framing: Scripture meets despair without flinching and without scolding. It records God's own people praying that they would rather die, and it answers not with a rebuke but with food, rest, and presence. Your life is not yours to throw away, and the darkness you are in is not the final word over you.
cultural: Elijah, just after his greatest victory, collapsed under a tree and begged God to take his life. Job cursed the day he was born. The Psalmist said darkness was his only friend. The biblical world made room for words this honest because it knew despair was real, and it never treated the suicidal cry as a sin to be hushed but as a soul to be reached.
historical: The church has not always handled despair well, sometimes adding shame to it, but its better tradition has insisted that the despairing are precious and never beyond rescue. Charles Spurgeon, the most famous preacher of the nineteenth century, spoke openly of being so low he wished he had never been born, and used his own darkness to reach others in theirs.
application: If you are thinking of ending your life, please reach out right now. In the US, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, available day and night, or go to your nearest emergency room. Tell one real person today, do not carry this alone, and let a doctor or counselor in. Hold on through this hour, then the next. The darkness is real, but it is not the truth about you, and it does not get the last word.

verses.text: Then He said to me, “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.’
verses.where: Ezekiel sees a valley of very dry bones, and God explains them: they are his people in exile, repeating a saying of despair, that their bones are dried up, their hope has perished, they are cut off. God does not argue with the saying. He answers it by promising to open their graves and put his Spirit in them.

verses.text: But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel. And besides all this, it is the third day since these things took place.
verses.where: Two disciples walk away from Jerusalem on the first Easter afternoon, telling a stranger that they had hoped Jesus was the one. Their hope is in the past tense. The stranger walking beside them is the risen Jesus, and they do not yet know it.

verses.text: For the Lord will not cast us off forever. Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion. For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.
verses.where: Lamentations was written over the ruins of Jerusalem. In the middle of its grief the writer holds on to three things about God: he does not cast off forever, his compassion follows the grief, and he does not afflict from his heart. Hope is built from what God is like, not from what the day looks like.

verses.text: But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.
verses.where: Israel in exile complains that its way is hidden from the LORD. Isaiah answers that the Creator never grows tired, and that even the strongest young people stumble. Those who wait for the LORD exchange their strength for his. The promise ends not with flying but with walking and not fainting.

verses.text: Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed and so became the father of many nations, just as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”
verses.where: Paul describes Abraham, old and childless, facing a promise that his body and Sarah's could not fulfill. Against all hope, in hope he believed. Paul does not say Abraham ignored the facts; he says Abraham faced them and trusted the God who gives life to the dead.

verses.text: But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.
verses.where: In the middle of his worst chapter, abandoned by family, friends and servants, Job wishes his words could be carved in rock forever. Then he says the thing he is most sure of: his Redeemer lives, and in the end he will see God with his own eyes. Hope here is not a mood but a claim held against everything around him.

verses.text: Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us.
verses.where: Paul writes to believers who already have peace with God. He traces a slow chain from suffering through endurance and character to hope, and says this hope does not disappoint. The reason is not our strength but the love God has already poured into our hearts by his Spirit.

verses.text: For in this hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see? But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.
verses.where: Paul has just described the whole creation groaning like a woman in labor, and believers groaning with it. Hope, he says, is for what is not yet seen. If it were already visible it would not be hope. So believers wait, patiently, while the groaning goes on.

verses.text: We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.
verses.where: Hebrews pictures hope as an anchor, firm and secure, but fixed in an unexpected place: behind the curtain in the inner sanctuary, where Jesus has already gone ahead. An anchor holds a ship that is still being tossed. The hope is secure because of where it is fastened, not because the water is calm.

verses.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you, who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.
verses.where: Peter writes to scattered Christians facing trials, and opens by praising God for a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus. It is called living because it rests on someone who was dead and is alive. The letter does not deny their grief; it says they rejoice even while they are distressed by various trials.

whole: If you have lost hope and are thinking of ending your life, please tell someone today, and if you are in danger, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Hopelessness can make it feel as if nothing would help. That feeling is part of the hopelessness, not a fact about your future.

Hope can drain away slowly or all at once: a diagnosis, a marriage that ended, a prayer unanswered for years, a long struggle that never seems to change. People describe it as waking up and seeing no reason the day should be different from the last one. For Christians, losing hope often brings shame as well, because they believe they are supposed to be people of hope, and they no longer feel it.

The Bible is not surprised by this. God's own people in exile said our hope has perished, and he quoted them, not to rebuke them but to answer them. Two disciples on the road to Emmaus spoke of hope in the past tense while the risen Jesus walked beside them. Abraham believed against all hope. The biblical word for hope is not optimism. It is not the feeling that things will get better. It is confidence in a person, the God who raises the dead, held while the facts still look the same.

That is why hope can be held even when it cannot be felt. It is borrowed at first, from people who still have it, from the psalms, from the testimony of others who have walked this road. It is fastened to something outside you, like an anchor behind the curtain. It grows slowly, Paul says, through endurance, not in an instant. So do the next small thing: tell someone, eat, sleep, see a doctor if the darkness is lasting, let someone pray for you when you cannot. You are not asked to manufacture hope. You are invited to hold on to the one who has not let go of you.
deep.sit: Who in your life still has hope for you, and could you let them hold it for a while?

prayer.lead: A prayer of an old believer who has seen many troubles and still expects to be brought back up. Pray it in the future tense, even if the present one is dark.
prayer.text: Though You have shown me many troubles and misfortunes, You will revive me once again. Even from the depths of the earth You will bring me back up. You will increase my honor and comfort me once again.

careLines.text: If you feel stuck and sinking, please tell someone you trust.
Despair is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country.
If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
